'''''Mimosa diplotricha''''' is a species of [[Fabaceae|leguminous]] woody shrub native to the [[Neotropics]]. It is an [[invasive species]] and now has a [[pantropical]] distribution.<ref name="PIER">Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER) (2007) PIER species lists, retrieved 4/30/2007 [http://www.hear.org/Pier/species/mimosa_diplotricha.htm ''Mimosa diplotricha'']</ref><ref name="lkcm">{{cite web
|url=http://lkcnhm.nus.edu.sg/dna/organisms/details/532
|title=''Mimosa diplotricha'' C.Wright 
|publisher=Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum. 
|access-date=16 November 2016
}}</ref> It is commonly known as the '''giant sensitive plant''', '''giant false sensitive plant''', or '''nila grass'''.<ref name="iucn">{{cite web
|url=http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=997
|title=''Mimosa diplotricha''
|author=Global Invasive Species Database
|publisher=International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)
|access-date=16 November 2016
}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Mimosa diplotricha'' is classified under the [[genus]] ''[[Mimosa]]'' in the [[subfamily (biology)|subfamily]] [[Mimosoideae]] of the [[legume]] [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[Fabaceae]]. It was first described by the American [[botanist]] [[Charles Wright (botanist)|Charles Wright]] in 1869. The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] is derived from [[Ancient Greek]] διπλόος (''diplóos'', "double") and θρίξ (''thríx'', "hair").<ref name="sauv">{{cite book
|author=Francisco A. Sauvalle
|editor =Antionio Mestre
|editor2 =Marcos de J. Melero
|title =Flora Cubana. Revisio Catalogi Grisebachiani vel Index Plantarum Cubensium
|publisher ="La Antilla" de Cacho-Negrete
|series =Anales de la Academia de Ciencias Médicas, Físicas y Naturales de la Habana
|volume=5
|year =1869
|pages=405–406
|url =https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/3669#/summary
}}</ref><ref name="tropicos">{{cite web
|url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/13022418
|title=''Mimosa diplotricha'' C. Wright ''ex'' Sauvalle
|author=Tropicos 
|date=16 November 2016
|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden
|access-date=16 November 2016
}}</ref>

''Mimosa diplotricha'' was also described earlier by the German botanist [[Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius]] as ''[[Mimosa invisa]]'' in 1837. But he had already given the name ''Mimosa invisa'' in 1834 to a different species. The name he gave is therefore a [[Heterotypic synonym|heterotypic]] posterior [[Homonym (biology)|homonym]] and thus ''[[nomen illegitimum]].'' Wright's name becomes the earliest correct name for the species, while the name ''Mimosa invisa'' is now accepted as the [[correct name]] for ''Mimosa rhodostachya''. However the name ''Mimosa invisa'' is still used incorrectly by some authors for ''Mimosa diplotricha.''<ref name="barneby">{{cite journal
|author=Rupert C. Barneby
|year=1987

}}</ref><ref name="cabi">{{cite web

''Mimosa diplotricha'' includes three [[variety (botany)|varieties]]:<ref name="barneby1991">{{cite journal|author=Rupert C. Barneby|year=1991|title= ''Sensitivae censitae:'' a description of the genus ''Mimosa'' Linnaeus (Mimosaceae) in the New World |journal=Memoirs of the New York Botanical Garden|volume=65|pages=1–835|url=http://antbase.org/ants/publications/nybg/Mimosa%20NY-Botanical_gardens_Vol.%2065%20-%20Copy.pdf}}</ref>
*''Mimosa diplotricha'' var. ''diplotricha'' <small>C. Wright ''ex'' Sauvalle</small>- The nominate variety. Characterized by seed pods that are {{convert|10|to|25|mm|in|abbr=on}} long, with 3 to 8 seeds.
*''Mimosa diplotricha'' var. ''odibilis'' <small>Barneby</small> - Found only in [[Mexico]], from [[Sinaloa]] to [[Michoacán]]. Characterized by seed pods that are {{convert|40|to|70|mm|in|abbr=on}} long, with 12 to 16 seeds.
* ''Mimosa diplotricha'' var. ''inermis'' <small>(Adelbert) Verdcourt</small> - A thornless variety found in tropical Asia. It appears to be a ''[[de novo (genetics)|de novo]]'' [[mutation]] that first arose in [[Indonesia]] and [[Papua New Guinea]].<ref name="Balbarino">{{cite book|author=Edwin A. Balbarino|author2=David M. ==Common names==
''Mimosa diplotricha'' is known as the giant sensitive plant, giant false sensitive plant, or nila grass in English.<ref name="fao"/>

In the [[Americas]], it is known ''dormilona de playa'', ''rabo de iguana''; and ''raspancilla'' in [[Spanish language|Spanish]]; and ''grande sensitive'' or ''sensitive géante'' in [[French language|French]]. It is also known as ''sensitiva trepadora'' in [[Cuba]]; and ''analeira'', ''dormideira'', ''juquiri-rasteiro'', ''malicia-de-mulher'', or ''sensitiva'' in [[Brazil]].<ref name="cabi"/>

In [[South Asia]] and [[Indochina]] it is known as ''anthottawadi'' or ''padaincha'' in [[India]]; ''banla saet'' in [[Cambodia]]; ''cõ trinh nu móc'' in [[Vietnam]]; and ''maiyaraap thao'' in [[Thailand]]. In [[Southeast Asia]] it is known as ''duri semalu'' in [[Malaysia]]; ''makahiyang lalaki'', ''bulunsari'', or ''balansuri'' in the [[Philippines]];  ''boring'', ''borang'', ''djoekoet borang'', or ''puteri malu'' in [[Nusa Tenggara]]; ''pis koetjing'' in [[Indonesia]]; and ''rèmbètè'' in [[Java]].

In [[Oceania]] it is known as nila grass in [[Papua New Guinea]]; ''co gadrogadro'', ''{{not a typo|wa ngandrongandro ni wa ngalelevu}}'', or ''{{not a typo|wa ngandrongandro levu}}'' in [[Fiji]]; ''vao fefe palagi'' or ''la'au fefe palagi'' in [[Samoa]] and the [[American Samoa]]; ''singbiguin sasa'' in [[Saipan]]; ''mechiuaiuu'' in [[Palau]]; and ''pikika'a papa'a'' in the [[Cook Islands]].<ref name="iucn"/><ref name="fao"/>

==Description==
[[File:Giant sensitive plant after touching.jpg|thumb|''Mimosa diplotricha'' leaves that have curled up after being touched]]
''Mimosa diplotricha'' grows as an erect shrub or a scrambling climber, reaching a height of around {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on}}. Its leaves are bipinnate and bright green with a feathery appearance. They are arranged alternately along the stems. Each leaf contains around twenty pairs of small sessile lanceolate leaflets arranged opposite each other. Each leaflet measures around {{convert|6|to|12|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.5|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide. Like the related ''[[Mimosa pudica]]'', the leaves are sensitive to touch, and will curl up if disturbed.<ref name="fao">{{cite book|author=Asia-Pacific Forest Invasive Species Network|title =''Mimosa diplotricha''|publisher =Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO)|series =Invasive Pest Fact Sheet|url =http://www.fao.org/forestry/13377-0977cb34791475aa6a7a360640f09778.pdf}}</ref>

The stems are characteristically very long. They are squarish in cross-section, with four ridges running lengthwise. A dense row of very sharp recurved thorns run along the ridges, each around {{convert|3|to|6|mm|in|abbr=on}} long. The [[flower]]s are pale pink and looks like a clustered fluffy ball. They are around {{convert|12|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter and arise from short stalks from the leaf joints. The corolla is fused (gamopetalous), and there are two stamens for every petal.<ref name="fao"/>

The flowers develop into clustered slightly curved seed pods. Each seed pod is more or less flat and covered with small prickles. They are around {{convert|10|to|35|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|6|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide. The seeds are oval-shaped and flat, each around {{convert|2|to|2.5|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.6|to|1.4|mm|in|abbr=on}} thick. They are light brown and polished in appearance. They are dispersed through running water or by sticking to fur or clothing. They can remain dormant for up to 50 years.<ref name="fao"/>

==Distribution==
''Mimosa diplotricha'' is native to the tropical and subtropical regions of [[South America]] and [[Central America]], including parts of the [[Caribbean]]. It is not known, however, if the species is native to [[North America]].<ref name="cabi"/>

==Invasive species==
''Mimosa diplotricha'' is fast-growing and can tolerate a wide range of soil and climate conditions. Left alone, they can form impenetrable thickets within a short period that can affect movement of both people and animals, as well as planted crops. All parts of the plant are toxic to grazing animals.<ref name="fao"/>

''Mimosa diplotricha'' is extremely [[invasive species|invasive]] and rapidly colonizes areas it is introduced to.<ref name="cabi"/> The earliest records of ''Mimosa diplotricha'' outside of the Americas is in [[Java]], [[Indonesia]] in 1900; [[Queensland]], [[Australia]] in 1929; and [[Fiji]] in 1936. Since then, it has rapidly spread and naturalized throughout [[Southeast Asia]], the [[Pacific Islands]] (including [[Hawaii]]), northern regions of [[Australia]], and parts of [[Africa]] in the latter half of the 20th century.<ref name="cabi"/>
